profile.summary: Joel is a short and intense prophecy addressed to Judah and Jerusalem in the midst of a devastating crisis. The book presents a land ruined by a plague of locusts and drought, a situation that threatens the survival of the people and the worship of the temple itself. Faced with the disaster, Joel calls the community to examine their condition before God, to abandon sin and to turn to the Lord with sincere repentance. The divine response comes in two directions: immediate restoration of the material life of the earth and, on a broader horizon, outpouring of the Spirit and judgment upon the nations. Joel's exact date and context are uncertain, but his message is widely recognized as valid for any time.
profile.setting: Joel prophesies for Judah and Jerusalem during an unprecedented national catastrophe: an infestation of locusts destroyed crops, vineyards, fruit trees and pastures, aggravated by severe drought. In the ancient world, without modern means of pest control or relief networks, this meant hunger, economic collapse and risk of death for many. The book does not clearly identify the king in exercise or the precise historical moment. Some place it early, before other prophets of the 8th century BC; others defend a later date, after exile, because of literary and historical indications. Uncertainty remains, but the text less emphasizes God's chronology and more sovereignty over the crisis.

structure.label: Title and announcement of the calamity
structure.description: Presentation of the prophecy and call to recognize the gravity of the disaster on earth and worship.

structure.label: Lord's Day, Repentance and Promise of Restoration
structure.description: Urgent call to repentance, followed by the divine response of compassion, restoration and promise of future renewal.

structure.label: Judgment of nations and consummation of hope
structure.description: God judges the enemy peoples and affirms his final government, bringing complete justice and restoration to his people.

themes: Sovereignty of God over nature, history and nations
Sincere repentance as an adequate response to divine discipline
Mercy and compassion of God toward those who turn to him
Lord's Day as God's Time of Judgment and Decisive Intervention
Material Restoration and Spiritual Renewal by the Spirit
readingKeys: Notice how natural disaster is not only treated as an accident, but as an occasion to discern God's sovereign action.
Note the difference between external religiosity and true repentance: the prophet's focus is on the contrite heart.
Follow the passage of the crisis present to the future promise, seeing how the book connects immediate restoration and eschatological hope.
profile.cautions: Joel's date is debated and should not be treated as right. The book has also been read in different ways: some understand the language of chapter 2 as a literal description of locusts, while others see it as the image of an invading army and the Lord's day. This introduction follows the line that highlights the crisis with locusts and the divine response, without solving all academic discussions.

dossier.narratedEra: Judah and Jerusalem in the time of an agricultural and cultured catastrophe: a plague of unprecedented locusts aggravated by drought, which threatens the survival of the land, the flocks and the worship of the temple (Jl 1:1-2:17). The very language of the notes also opens up the possibility that Joel is describing, with images of plague, the imminence of the Lord's day and/or a future invasion, but the immediate scenario narrated is Judah in crisis.
dossier.compositionEra: The date of composition is uncertain. Tyndale's introduction notes present most scholars as inclined to a post-exile date, although they recognize proposals of ancient date, until Joash's reign during the king's minority under Joiada's supervision. Matthew Henry also claims total uncertainty, but judges likely a time close to that of Amos. Thus, the composition is debated between a date prior to exile and a post-exile; the sources do not allow exact fixation.

politics.title: Monarchy of Judah not explained, but possibly in the context of Joash
politics.detail: The introduction of Tyndale notes that Joel does not mention the kings under whom he ministered; some interpreters put him in the time of Joash (835-796 BC), when the kingdom would be under the priest Joiada, precisely because the book does not criticize the monarchy and sees the priesthood favorably.
politics.readingImpact: If this ancient reading is correct, the book gains the weight of a prophetic word in a monarchical context still in force, with strong priestly protagonism in the temple. If not, this absence of kings prevents the tie the message to a specific reign.

politics.title: End of the northern kingdom and absence of Samaria
politics.detail: Tyndale notes that Joel does not mention the northern kingdom or Samaria, which leads many to place it after the destruction of Northern Israel in 722 BC.
politics.readingImpact: This shifts the reading to a horizon in which the political separation between north and south is no longer the center of the problem; the focus becomes Judah as remaining people under their own threat.

politics.title: Assyrian and Babylon absent as contemporary enemies
politics.detail: The notes state that Joel does not mention Assyria or Babylonia, and several interpreters understand this as an indication that these empires were already much outside the political horizon of the prophet, favoring a later date from the centuries VIII-IVI B.C.
politics.readingImpact: The absence of these empires pushes the reading to a period when the crisis of Judah is presented without the classical framing of the great threatening powers, reinforcing the universality of divine judgment.

politics.title: Foreign peoples such as oppressors and slave traffickers
politics.detail: In chapter 3, nations, especially Tyre, Sidon, and Philistia, are accused of plundering Jerusalem and selling Jews as slaves to the Greeks; Egypt and Edom are also cited as ancient enemies subject to judgment.
politics.readingImpact: The political context ceases to be only domestic: the book reads the history of Judah in relation to foreign empires and city-states that exploit the people of the covenant. This reinforces the international dimension of God's judgment.

politics.title: The nations gathered for judgment in 'vale of Jesafá'
politics.detail: The notes identify the "vale of Jehoshaphat" as a symbolic name, not linked to King Jehoshaphat of Judah, but to the place where the Lord will judge the nations. The scene is of military gathering and divine decision on the peoples.
politics.readingImpact: World politics is subordinate to the court of God. Reading shifts the attention of human covenants to the divine verdict on entire nations.

customs.title: Cult in the temple interrupted by hunger
customs.detail: The plague and drought prevent the regular offers of cereal and wine, and the text highlights that there was even lack for the daily offerings in the temple of Jerusalem.
customs.readingImpact: Disaster is not just economic; it affects the center of the religious life of Judah. Reading shows that repentance and restoration also involve the reintegration of sacrificial cult.

customs.title: Public mourning and solemn fasting as a community response
customs.detail: The priests shall summon the elders and all the people to public rites of mourning, fasting and solemn assembly in the temple. The notes mention tearing up the garments as a common gesture of grief in the ancient world, but insist that this should correspond to inner change.
customs.readingImpact: The proper response to the disaster is community, liturgical and moral, non-indisponse. The reader realizes that Joel transforms calamity into a penitential assembly.

customs.title: The family and the daily life of agriculture affected by the plague
customs.detail: The notes describe the destruction of gardens, grains, vineyards, fruit trees and even the pastures of sheep and goats. In 1:8, Judah is compared to a young bride whose marriage becomes unfeasible for mourning; in 2:16, bride and newlyweds are also summoned to the temple in national emergency.
customs.readingImpact: Domestic life, marriage and food appear as vulnerable to the crisis. This intensifies pastoral reading: the message reaches marriage, table and work of the field, not only formal religion.

customs.title: Agrarian economy based on grain, wine and olive oil
customs.detail: The notes underline that the three essential foods of ancient Israel were grain, wine and olive oil; their loss means hunger and paralysis of the rural economy. In 2:18-27, divine restoration includes again these products and herds.
customs.readingImpact: The book presupposes an agrarian economy dependent on crops and cattle. The restoration promised by God is concrete, material and visible, not just spiritual.

customs.title: Fage and daily consumption of food and drink
customs.detail: The notes mention the cry of sheep and goats for lack of pasture, and observe that the plague and drought have left empty barns and the land without water. They also highlight the restoration of "new wine" and "ozeite" as a sign of renewed provision.
customs.readingImpact: The daily livelihood of humans and animals is intertwined. This helps the reader to see that Joel deals with basic survival, not religious abstractions.

language.title: The "Member of the Lord" as an expression of judgment
language.detail: The notes explain that disaster is a sign that the Lord's day is near; it is not merely a natural event. In 2:2, the day is described as "darkness and darkness," in contrast to popular expectations of automatic blessing.
language.readingImpact: Language redefines the meaning of the crisis: calamity requires theological discernment, not only social reaction. The reader is forced to face judgment and responsibility.

language.title: Image of swarm as an army
language.detail: Tyndale notes that in 2:1-11, some read the text as an apocalyptic description of a human invasion, using the language of the plague. The text compares the locusts to horses, describes the bang as deafening and advances them as a disciplined army that scales walls.
language.readingImpact: The military image extends reading: the plague is not only biological, but also a sign of a divine war. This prepares the call to repentance.

language.title: Inverted creation language: Eden and desolation
language.detail: The notes say that before the devastation, the land looked like the garden of Eden, but then becomes desolation. They also claim that the sun, moon, and earth that tremble are typical signs of theophany and judgment.
language.readingImpact: Joel uses cosmic images to show that sin affects the created order. The reader understands the local disaster as an echo of a broader collapse of creation before God.

language.title: "Rasgai the heart" and the interiority of penance
language.detail: The notes highlight that the heart, in Hebrew, is the center of thought, faith and will, and that Joel summons the inner change, not only external gestures such as tearing the garments.
language.readingImpact: Prophetic language corrects formalism: true repentance is internal transformation. This changes the reading of the cult and spiritual discipline.

language.title: Sound repetition and agricultural metaphors in the judgment of nations
language.detail: In chapter 3, the expression "crowds," crowds" is explained as a Hebrew repetition that mimics the chaos of the crowd. The judgment is described by sickle images about the cereal and the dirty footsteps of the mill.
language.readingImpact: Language reinforces the inevitability and violence of divine judgment. For the reader, the defeat of nations is presented with rural images familiar to an agrarian society.

timeline.title: Early catastrophe of grassland and drought in Judah
timeline.detail: The book begins with a devastating plague that destroys crops, vineyards and trees, and drought deepens the crisis. The notes deal with this as the immediate historical situation of Judah and Jerusalem.
timeline.readingImpact: This initial milestone conditions all prophecy: the calls to repentance are born from a real crisis of hunger and cult interrupted.

timeline.title: Urgent call to repentance before full judgment
timeline.detail: Joel 2:12-17 is presented as a window still open to return to the Lord before the final destruction. The appeal comes immediately after the description of the threatening advance.
timeline.readingImpact: The moral chronology of the book is urgent: there is still time, but little. This gives pastoral weight to the call to the assembly, fasting and intercession.

timeline.title: Immediate material restitution after the divine response
timeline.detail: If there is sincere repentance, God will restore fields, orchards, vineyards, rains, and flocks. The notes present this restoration as close and concrete.
timeline.readingImpact: Biblical hope is not abstract; it includes harvest, rain, and abundance. The reader must expect a redemption that reaches material life.

timeline.title: Cosmic signs and outpouring of the Spirit were given in the distant future
timeline.detail: The notes distinguish a more remote horizon in which God will pour out his Spirit on "all flesh," with signs in heaven and universal call to the Lord. Tyndale relates this to Pentecost as a fulfillment in Acts 2.
timeline.readingImpact: The prophetic time expands: from an immediate agricultural crisis to a eschatological and pneumological hope. This allows you to read Joel as a bridge between local restoration and future wider redeemer.

timeline.title: Future Judgment on the Oppressive Nations
timeline.detail: The nations that plundered Jerusalem and trafficked their people will be gathered together for judgment in the valley of Jehoshaphat. The scene includes Egypt and Edom as targets of the final judgment.
timeline.readingImpact: The story does not end in the pain of Judah; there is an international account. The reader sees that God responds to historical violence against his people.

timeline.title: Date of composition debated between pre-exyl and post-exile period
timeline.detail: Tyndale records an ancient proposal linked to the reign of Joash and another, now majority among post-exile scholars, after the return of 538 BC. Matthew Henry only says that time is uncertain and probable contemporary of Amos.
timeline.readingImpact: Uncertainty prevents using Joel as a closed chronological piece; reading should focus on the theological and literary message, not on rigid dates.

investigation: Is the plague of locusts described as a concrete historical event or as an apocalyptic language for a human army? Notes record both readings, without definitively resolving.
Should the mention of four types of locusts in 1:4 be read as stages of the insect or as four empires? Tyndale presents the second option only as an interpretation of some commentators.
The relationship between Joel and other prophets is Joel's literary dependence on Amos, Zephaniah, Obadiah and Ezekiel, or the reverse? The introduction admits both possibilities.

Does the favorable use of the temple and priesthood in Joel reflect a post-exile emphasis or simply the specific situation of the book? The sources suggest an association with the post-exile phase, but without conclusive proof.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends solely on the notes provided and is therefore selective. There is no firm data on kings, empires or events that have been accurately dated in the text itself; the chronological proposals appear as hypotheses, not as certainty. There is also important interpretative controversy in Jl 2:1-11 between literal plague and figurative description of invasion. The notes deal with temple customs, mourning, food and agriculture in more detail than family or social classes themes, so the customs section was concentrated on these points. No external contexts, etymologies or historical reconstructions not explained in the sources were added.
